screens.title: $match Stage — Definition and Purpose
screens.narratorSegment: The $match stage is a filter that accepts the same query language you use in find operations, but inside an aggregation pipeline. That means you can use range operators like greater than and less than, list membership operators like in and nin, logical combinators such as and, or, and not, and even regular expression matching for text patterns. A clear claim: when you can reduce the number of documents early with $match, subsequent stages have less work to do and your pipeline runs faster. For example, if you only need login events for a single user after a certain date, write a $match that includes type equals login, userId equals the user, and timestamp greater than your cutoff. A common misconception is that multiple $match stages are expensive; in practice you can have several matches, and placing the most selective conditions early is the optimization. Remember to prefer indexable predicates inside $match so MongoDB can use an index scan, which is far faster than scanning the full collection. To check your understanding: can you express a filter that finds documents where amount is greater than 100 and currency is USD using $match? That is the exact kind of filter $match is designed for.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › $match Stage
Definition

$match filters documents using MongoDB's query operators. Use it to express ranges, lists, logical conditions, and patterns.

Common operators
  • $gt, $lt, $gte, $lte for ranges
  • $in, $nin for list membership
  • $and, $or, $not for logical composition
  • $regex for simple pattern matches
Example
db.events.aggregate([
  { $match: {
      type: "login",
      userId: "userA",
      timestamp: { $gte: ISODate("2023-01-06T00:00:00Z") },
      durationMs: { $gt: 50 }
    }
  }
])
Misconception

Putting $match late is ok if you need transformed fields first — but if you can filter earlier, do so to reduce work.

Practical tips
  • Combine multiple conditions inside a single $match for clarity and index use.
  • Prefer simple equality and range predicates that align with existing indexes.
  • Use $regex sparingly inside $match since it may not use indexes unless anchored.
Key Takeaway

Write selective, indexable $match predicates early to reduce documents flowing through the pipeline.

screens.title: Operators Inside $match
screens.narratorSegment: Inside a $match stage you use the same operators you would in a query. Range queries use operators like greater than, less than, greater or equal, and less or equal to find numeric or date intervals. List-based filters use in to accept any of a set of values, and nin to exclude a set. Logical composition uses and, or, and not to combine predicates when a single field alone is not sufficient. Regular expressions allow pattern matching, useful for text fields but often less index‑friendly unless anchored. A practical sequence: start by writing the simplest equalities and ranges that can use indexes, then layer in or groups when you must accept multiple alternatives. A common mistake is to overuse or with many alternatives when an index exists on a single field — this can reduce index effectiveness. Concretely, to find events where type is login and duration is greater than 50 and the timestamp is after a date, you combine those three predicates in one $match document. When you practice in labs, test whether the predicate uses an index by examining the query plan; if it doesn't, restructure the predicate or add a compound index that matches your filter and sort keys.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › $match Operators
Step-by-step operator guide
Ranges: $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte for numbers and dates.
Lists: $in and $nin select or exclude sets of values.
Logic: $and, $or, $not combine predicates for complex rules.
Patterns: $regex for text; anchor when you need index use.
Example: combined
db.events.aggregate([
  { $match: {
      $and: [
        { type: 'login' },
        { timestamp: { $gte: ISODate('2023-01-01') } },
        { durationMs: { $gt: 50 } }
      ]
    }
  }
])
Practical checklist
  • Start with equality or range predicates that match an index.
  • Avoid wide $or lists when a more selective predicate exists.
  • Use $regex only when necessary and test whether it uses an index.
Common mistake

Assuming any $regex will use an index; unanchored patterns often prevent index scans and slow queries.

screens.title: Placement & Indexing — Performance Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Performance in aggregation often comes down to two decisions: where you place $match and whether the predicates can use an index. Placing $match as early as possible reduces the number of documents that downstream stages like $sort, $group, and $project must handle. Less data means lower memory use and faster execution. Index alignment matters because if your match and sort keys are covered by a compound index, MongoDB can often use an index scan that returns already-sorted documents, eliminating an expensive in‑memory sort. A critical constraint to remember is MongoDB's 100MB memory limit for in‑memory sorts inside aggregation stages; if your sort needs more memory, the server may fail the pipeline unless allowDiskUse is enabled, which has its own cost. A common error is to write complex transformations before a $match when a simple filter could run first. If you must transform documents to compute a value you need to filter on, keep the transformation minimal and consider whether an index or a precomputed field is a better choice. Check the query plan to confirm whether the index was used and, if not, adjust the predicate or index design.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Placement & Indexing
Why $match early?

Filtering earlier reduces data volume, which reduces CPU, memory, and I/O for later stages.

Index alignment

If match and sort keys match a compound index, MongoDB can satisfy the sort from the index and avoid memory‑heavy operations.

Memory limit

In‑memory sorts have a 100MB limit; large sorts need allowDiskUse or index coverage.

Checklist before running a heavy pipeline
  • Can you move $match earlier to cut documents?
  • Do your match and sort fields appear in an index?
  • Will the sort operate on too many documents?
Quick example
// Compound index suggestion
{ category: 1, price: -1 }
Key Takeaway

Think about selectivity and index coverage up front. An early selective $match and a matching index make sorts cheap.

screens.title: Example: Filtering events for a user
screens.narratorSegment: Let's step through a real example using an events collection with fields like type, userId, timestamp, and durationMs. Suppose we need all login events for a particular user after a cutoff time and only where duration is greater than a threshold. The single $match stage combines these predicates, which keeps the pipeline simple and maximizes index use if userId and timestamp are indexed. The sample pipeline filters on type equals login, userId equals userA, timestamp greater or equal to a specific date, and durationMs greater than 50. When you run this pipeline, look at the explain output to verify an index was used; if not, add an index or restructure the predicate. A common misconception is that splitting conditions across multiple stages will always be faster — it won't if the split stops the optimizer from using a single index. Finally, test such filters against representative data volumes to confirm the plan and runtime. Practically, this pattern is the building block for queries like retrieving recent activity for a user in a dashboard or audit view. Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Events Example
Starter documents
{ "_id": 1, "type": "login", "userId": "userA", "timestamp": ISODate("2023-01-05T10:00:00Z"), "durationMs": 100 }
{ "_id": 4, "type": "login", "userId": "userA", "timestamp": ISODate("2023-01-06T09:00:00Z"), "durationMs": 90 }
Pipeline
db.events.aggregate([
  { $match: {
      type: "login",
      userId: "userA",

    }

Explanation
  • type and userId are exact matches for quick filtering.
  • timestamp is a range predicate that can use a date index.
  • durationMs filters out null or short events.
Key Takeaway

Combine predicates inside one $match and confirm index usage with explain to keep pipelines efficient.

screens.title: $sort Stage — Ordering Documents
screens.narratorSegment: The $sort stage reorders documents according to one or more specified fields. Each field in the sort document has a value of 1 for ascending or -1 for descending. When you specify multiple fields, the order of keys determines primary, secondary, and further sort priorities. For instance, sorting by category ascending and price descending groups documents by category and then orders items within each category from highest to lowest price. One practical point: sort must operate on the documents passed to it, so if you need the top results by a metric, put the $sort before $limit to ensure you limit the sorted results rather than an arbitrary subset. Performance-wise, if your match predicates and sort keys are served by an index, MongoDB can scan the index in sort order and avoid loading data into memory. A common pitfall is relying on sort without a matching index for large datasets; this can trigger an in‑memory sort and potentially exceed memory limits. When designing APIs or dashboards, decide which fields are most commonly used for sorting and ensure proper indexing to keep response times low.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › $sort Stage
How $sort works

Specify fields with 1 or -1. Order of keys determines priority when multiple fields are present.

Example
db.events.aggregate([
  { $match: { type: "login", userId: "userA" } },
  { $sort: { timestamp: -1 } } // most recent first
])
Performance notes
  • A sort that can use an index avoids large in‑memory operations.
  • Sort before limit to ensure you limit the ordered set, not an arbitrary subset.
  • Large sorts may hit the 100MB limit unless allowDiskUse is enabled.
Key Takeaway

Choose sort keys and indexes together so ordering is fast and deterministic.

screens.title: $limit Stage — Controlling Result Size
screens.narratorSegment: The $limit stage simply caps the number of documents that continue through the pipeline. It is indispensable for top‑N queries, early exits, and controlling response sizes for APIs. Importantly, $limit should appear after $sort when you want to retrieve the top results according to an ordering. If you place $limit before $sort, you will cap an arbitrary subset of documents and lose deterministic ordering. For example, after filtering in $match and ordering with $sort, $limit: 3 will return the three highest scoring documents. A subtlety: $limit reduces work downstream, so placing it early — once the results are properly ordered — can save processing. When building paginated endpoints, $limit is paired with $skip to take a window of the ordered results, but $skip becomes inefficient at large offsets because the server still has to traverse and discard skipped documents. For very large collections prefer cursor-based paging, using the last seen sort key to fetch the next page without heavy skipping. Always think about what you want to cap — the whole collection or the sorted set — and place $limit accordingly.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › $limit Stage
What $limit does

Returns at most N documents to the next stage or the client, useful for top‑N and paging windows.

Top‑N pattern
db.products.aggregate([
  { $match: { category: 'Electronics', inStock: true } },
  { $sort: { price: -1 } },
  { $limit: 3 }
])
Pagination note

$limit with $skip provides offset paging, but skip can be expensive for large offsets because documents are still processed and discarded.

Key Takeaway

Use $limit to bound sorted sets. For high offsets, prefer cursor-based pagination using the last seen sort key.

screens.title: Top‑N Query: Most Expensive Electronics
screens.narratorSegment: Let's combine the three stages into a compact pipeline that finds the top three most expensive in‑stock electronics items. First, $match filters category equals Electronics and inStock equals true. This reduces the dataset to relevant products. Next, $sort orders by price descending so the highest priced items appear first. Finally, $limit returns the first three documents from that ordered stream. The order matters: if you limit before sorting, you could return three arbitrary products and then sort them, which is not the desired result. For performance, a compound index on category ascending and price descending covers both the filter and the order, allowing an index scan that avoids an in‑memory sort. If your index differs, the database may have to read many documents and perform an expensive sort. Test with explain to see whether the index was used and consider building a compound index when top‑N queries are common. This pattern maps directly to features like leaderboards, top selling lists, and featured product selections. Top‑N Query: Most Expensive Electronics means match to narrow the set, sort the set in the desired order, then limit to the top n — align indexes to avoid in‑memory sorts.. In practical terms, combine $match, $sort, and $limit to return the top 3 items.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Top‑N Example
Pipeline
db.products.aggregate([

screens.title: Pagination with $skip and $limit
screens.narratorSegment: Pagination commonly uses $sort to define a deterministic order, then $skip and $limit to take an offset window. The typical pattern for page two of size ten is to sort by the desired key, skip ten rows, and limit to ten rows. The critical requirement is that you must sort first; otherwise skip and limit will return non-deterministic subsets. A practical performance caveat is that $skip is inefficient for large offsets because MongoDB still processes and discards the skipped documents, consuming C P U and memory. For very large collections or deep paging, cursor-based pagination is recommended: record the last seen sort key and use a filter like greater-than that value to fetch the next page, which avoids skip costs. Another common mistake is to paginate without a stable sort key; always ensure the sort order is deterministic so pages don't shift between requests. When designing an A P I, choose page sizes and strategies that balance user needs with backend efficiency and prefer cursor paging for high-volume use cases. screens.title: Skip vs Cursor Paging — Tradeoffs
screens.narratorSegment: Offset paging with $skip is simple and works well for small page numbers, but it becomes increasingly costly as the skip value grows because the database still processes and discards the skipped documents. Cursor-based pagination avoids that cost by using a stable sort key and a predicate that finds documents greater than the last seen value, returning the next window directly. A tradeoff is that cursor paging requires you to carry the last seen key between requests and to ensure stable deterministic ordering, typically by including a unique tiebreaker like an identifier. If you must support arbitrary deep pages or random access to page numbers, skip may be unavoidable, but consider limiting maximum page depth or use search cursors in your A P I to avoid heavy server work. For many real-world scenarios such as infinite scroll or feed loading, cursor paging is both faster and more consistent. Finally, always sort before skipping; skipping without a deterministic order produces inconsistent results that will confuse users. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll build a practical understanding of three aggregation stages that appear in almost every pipeline: match for filtering, sort for ordering, and limit for capping results. You'll learn the full range of query operators available inside a match stage, how sort accepts multiple keys and orders, and when and why to place these stages early in a pipeline to improve performance. We will run concrete examples using collections like events, products, and transactions so you can see end-to-end pipelines for top‑N queries and pagination. You will also get common performance checks such as index usage, memory limits for in‑memory sorts, and the pitfalls of using skip at large offsets. By the end you should be able to write aggregation pipelines that reliably return the right slice of data, understand when the database will leverage an index, and design efficient top‑N and paged queries. Think about a dashboard that needs the five most recent logins — the patterns here let you build that query both correctly and efficiently.

Over the next screens you will gain four core competencies that are essential for efficient aggregation queries. First, you will master $match to write advanced filters using range, list, logical, and pattern operators so you can limit documents precisely. Second, you will apply $sort to order documents by one or more fields, understanding primary and secondary sort keys and how order affects deterministic results. Third, you will use $limit to control how many documents pass through a pipeline, enabling top‑N queries and response sizing. Fourth, you will combine $match, $sort, and $limit to implement efficient pagination and top‑N patterns, while learning placement and index strategies that keep pipelines fast. Each objective includes a short practical mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you know when you have achieved it. These skills will help you build dashboards, APIs, and analytics that return consistent and fast results even on large collections.

These secondary objectives focus on the practical checks and operators you will use every day. You will learn the specific query operators that work inside $match — such as greater than, less than, in lists, logical combinations, and regular expressions — so you can express complex filters. You will also practice designing indexes that match the fields you filter and sort on so MongoDB can use index scans instead of expensive in‑memory sorts. Finally, you will gain awareness of skip's limitations on large offsets and explore alternatives like cursor‑based paging. Each objective includes a simple mnemonic to help you remember the sequence and a verified milestone so you can confirm your competency in a lab or interview. These objectives ensure you not only write correct pipelines but also reason about their cost and scalability.

The $match stage is a filter that accepts the same query language you use in find operations, but inside an aggregation pipeline. That means you can use range operators like greater than and less than, list membership operators like in and nin, logical combinators such as and, or, and not, and even regular expression matching for text patterns. A clear claim: when you can reduce the number of documents early with $match, subsequent stages have less work to do and your pipeline runs faster. For example, if you only need login events for a single user after a certain date, write a $match that includes type equals login, userId equals the user, and timestamp greater than your cutoff. A common misconception is that multiple $match stages are expensive; in practice you can have several matches, and placing the most selective conditions early is the optimization. Remember to prefer indexable predicates inside $match so MongoDB can use an index scan, which is far faster than scanning the full collection. To check your understanding: can you express a filter that finds documents where amount is greater than 100 and currency is USD using $match? That is the exact kind of filter $match is designed for.

Inside a $match stage you use the same operators you would in a query. Range queries use operators like greater than, less than, greater or equal, and less or equal to find numeric or date intervals. List-based filters use in to accept any of a set of values, and nin to exclude a set. Logical composition uses and, or, and not to combine predicates when a single field alone is not sufficient. Regular expressions allow pattern matching, useful for text fields but often less index‑friendly unless anchored. A practical sequence: start by writing the simplest equalities and ranges that can use indexes, then layer in or groups when you must accept multiple alternatives. A common mistake is to overuse or with many alternatives when an index exists on a single field — this can reduce index effectiveness. Concretely, to find events where type is login and duration is greater than 50 and the timestamp is after a date, you combine those three predicates in one $match document. When you practice in labs, test whether the predicate uses an index by examining the query plan; if it doesn't, restructure the predicate or add a compound index that matches your filter and sort keys.

Performance in aggregation often comes down to two decisions: where you place $match and whether the predicates can use an index. Placing $match as early as possible reduces the number of documents that downstream stages like $sort, $group, and $project must handle. Less data means lower memory use and faster execution. Index alignment matters because if your match and sort keys are covered by a compound index, MongoDB can often use an index scan that returns already-sorted documents, eliminating an expensive in‑memory sort. A critical constraint to remember is MongoDB's 100MB memory limit for in‑memory sorts inside aggregation stages; if your sort needs more memory, the server may fail the pipeline unless allowDiskUse is enabled, which has its own cost. A common error is to write complex transformations before a $match when a simple filter could run first. If you must transform documents to compute a value you need to filter on, keep the transformation minimal and consider whether an index or a precomputed field is a better choice. Check the query plan to confirm whether the index was used and, if not, adjust the predicate or index design.

Let's step through a real example using an events collection with fields like type, userId, timestamp, and durationMs. Suppose we need all login events for a particular user after a cutoff time and only where duration is greater than a threshold. The single $match stage combines these predicates, which keeps the pipeline simple and maximizes index use if userId and timestamp are indexed. The sample pipeline filters on type equals login, userId equals userA, timestamp greater or equal to a specific date, and durationMs greater than 50. When you run this pipeline, look at the explain output to verify an index was used; if not, add an index or restructure the predicate. A common misconception is that splitting conditions across multiple stages will always be faster — it won't if the split stops the optimizer from using a single index. Finally, test such filters against representative data volumes to confirm the plan and runtime. Practically, this pattern is the building block for queries like retrieving recent activity for a user in a dashboard or audit view. Example: Filtering events for a user means a single selective $match on userid, timestamp, and type keeps pipelines fast and predictable when indexes exist.. In practical terms, step through a real events collection query to see $match in action.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The $sort stage reorders documents according to one or more specified fields. Each field in the sort document has a value of 1 for ascending or -1 for descending. When you specify multiple fields, the order of keys determines primary, secondary, and further sort priorities. For instance, sorting by category ascending and price descending groups documents by category and then orders items within each category from highest to lowest price. One practical point: sort must operate on the documents passed to it, so if you need the top results by a metric, put the $sort before $limit to ensure you limit the sorted results rather than an arbitrary subset. Performance-wise, if your match predicates and sort keys are served by an index, MongoDB can scan the index in sort order and avoid loading data into memory. A common pitfall is relying on sort without a matching index for large datasets; this can trigger an in‑memory sort and potentially exceed memory limits. When designing APIs or dashboards, decide which fields are most commonly used for sorting and ensure proper indexing to keep response times low.

The $limit stage simply caps the number of documents that continue through the pipeline. It is indispensable for top‑N queries, early exits, and controlling response sizes for APIs. Importantly, $limit should appear after $sort when you want to retrieve the top results according to an ordering. If you place $limit before $sort, you will cap an arbitrary subset of documents and lose deterministic ordering. For example, after filtering in $match and ordering with $sort, $limit: 3 will return the three highest scoring documents. A subtlety: $limit reduces work downstream, so placing it early — once the results are properly ordered — can save processing. When building paginated endpoints, $limit is paired with $skip to take a window of the ordered results, but $skip becomes inefficient at large offsets because the server still has to traverse and discard skipped documents. For very large collections prefer cursor-based paging, using the last seen sort key to fetch the next page without heavy skipping. Always think about what you want to cap — the whole collection or the sorted set — and place $limit accordingly.

This reduces the dataset to relevant products. Next, $sort orders by price descending so the highest priced items appear first. If your index differs, the database may have to read many documents and perform an expensive sort. Test with explain to see whether the index was used and consider building a compound index when top‑N queries are common. Cursor-based pagination avoids that cost by using a stable sort key and a predicate that finds documents greater than the last seen value, returning the next window directly. A tradeoff is that cursor paging requires you to carry the last seen key between requests and to ensure stable deterministic ordering, typically by including a unique tiebreaker like an identifier. If you must support arbitrary deep pages or random access to page numbers, skip may be unavoidable, but consider limiting maximum page depth or use search cursors in your A P I to avoid heavy server work. For many real-world scenarios such as infinite scroll or feed loading, cursor paging is both faster and more consistent. Finally, always sort before skipping; skipping without a deterministic order produces inconsistent results that will confuse users.
